common_name: Little Beauty Kousa Dogwood (Compact Dwarf Chinese Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Beauty stays under 15 feet tall, making it one of the few kousa dogwoods that fits comfortably into a small yard or foundation bed.

directions: Site Little Beauty where its dense, multi-stemmed canopy of small white spring flowers can be viewed up close, since its reduced scale suits patios and entry gardens better than most full-sized kousa selections. Keep soil evenly moist and mulched, especially through the first two seasons, and prune only lightly to shape, since flowering occurs on wood set the previous year. Expect red, raspberry-like fruit to follow bloom and draw songbirds into late summer. Like other kousa dogwoods it resists the anthracnose and borer problems that plague native flowering dogwood in humid regions.

common_name: Lustgarten Weeping Kousa Dogwood (Elizabeth Lustgarten Weeping Chinese Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; this cultivar's cascading branch structure needs open space to arch downward unobstructed.

directions: This selection's branches cascade toward the ground in a rounded mound rather than growing upright, so stake or train a young plant if a taller weeping form is wanted, or let it sprawl naturally as a groundcover-scale specimen. Creamy bracts open in late spring and age to a soft pink blush, followed later by crimson fruit that persists into fall alongside red-orange foliage color. The exfoliating, mottled bark becomes an added feature as the trunk matures, giving winter interest long after leaves drop. Water deeply during establishment and avoid heavy pruning, since cutting back the weeping habit removes the following year's flower wood.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

common_name: Summer Fun Kousa Dogwood (White-Margined Variegated Chinese Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates; strong sun combined with drought stress can scorch the crisp white leaf margins on this variegated cultivar.

directions: Grown chiefly for its foliage, Summer Fun carries broad, irregular white margins around gray-green leaf centers that often blush pink in spring and again as fall approaches, when the whole canopy can flush fiery pink over a dark red interior. Give it consistent moisture and a site sheltered from harsh midday sun, particularly in warmer zones, to keep the variegated margins from browning. Small cream and white flower clusters appear in early summer, followed by edible, strawberry-textured red fruit that birds readily take. This selection also shows notably better resistance to verticillium wilt than many woody ornamentals, an advantage on sites with a history of the disease.

common_name: Temple Jewel Kousa Dogwood (Chartreuse Variegated Chinese Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in mostly sun to partial shade; give the canopy room to spread wide, since this cultivar grows broader than it is tall as it matures.

directions: New growth on Temple Jewel emerges with irregular lime-green and cream blotches at the leaf centers that gradually mature toward solid green by midsummer, giving the tree a two-toned look each spring. Large, long-lasting white bracts open in June and can remain showy for several weeks, followed by red, pulpy fruit that attracts birds into fall. The mottled gray-brown bark becomes an ornamental feature on older wood, so avoid crowding the trunk with mulch or nearby plantings. This selection also carries useful resistance to verticillium wilt, a plus on replant sites.

common_name: Big Apple Kousa Dogwood (Large-Fruited Chinese Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in any well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and allow generous room for this cultivar's eventual 20- to 30-foot spread.

directions: Big Apple earns its name from unusually large red fruit, up to an inch and a half across, that weighs down branches by late summer and draws heavy bird activity. Wide, overlapping white bracts cover the tree in late spring above dark green, heavily textured foliage that turns scarlet in autumn. Because it eventually reaches full shade-tree proportions, reserve it for a spot with room to grow rather than a tight foundation planting. Established plants tolerate brief dry spells but perform best with regular moisture and a layer of mulch to keep roots cool.

common_name: Galilean Kousa Dogwood (Large-Leaf Chinese Kousa Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with consistent summer moisture, in part shade to full sun; this vase-shaped selection, sold under the trade name Galilean, eventually needs a wide, open site.

directions: Galilean stands out for foliage roughly twice the size of typical kousa dogwood leaves, giving the canopy a bold, coarse texture that turns deep purple to orange-red in fall. Abundant white flower bracts open in early summer and hold their display for weeks, followed by large, strawberry-like red fruit. As it matures into a broad, vase-shaped small tree, the peeling gray-brown bark adds cold-season interest. Like most kousa selections it shows much better resistance to anthracnose than native flowering dogwood, making it a durable specimen or accent choice.

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in free-draining, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the oversized flower bracts show best with at least a half day of direct sun.

directions: Moonbeam is grown for exceptionally large, cream-white bracts tipped in pink that open after the leaves emerge, producing a flower display noticeably larger than most kousa cultivars. A rounded, well-proportioned habit develops as the tree matures into a 15- to 25-foot specimen, followed by red fruit and maroon-red fall color. It shares the kousa dogwood's tolerance for verticillium wilt and its resistance to the anthracnose that troubles native flowering dogwood in humid climates. Water regularly during the first two seasons and mulch to conserve soil moisture around the root zone.

common_name: China Girl Kousa Dogwood (Tiered-Branch Chinese Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered site in fall or spring in any well-drained, reasonably moist soil in full sun to partial shade; the tiered branching habit is most attractive when the tree isn't crowded by nearby plantings.

directions: China Girl builds a slow-growing, architectural framework of horizontally tiered branches that reads as a strong winter silhouette even without leaves. Upward-facing, creamy-yellow bracts appear in June, often most abundantly after a hot preceding summer, and give way to bright red, strawberry-like fruit that is decorative but not palatable. This Dutch-bred selection is notable for flowering reliably while still young, unlike some kousa cultivars that take years to reach bloom size. Deep green summer foliage finishes the season with strong red and orange fall color, and the tree performs best on a sheltered site with consistently moist, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Aurora is a Rutgers-bred hybrid selected for vigor and heavy bloom on a large-growing framework.

directions: Bred at Rutgers University by crossing native flowering dogwood with Asian kousa dogwood, Aurora grows more vigorously and reaches a larger mature size than most flowering dogwood cultivars, eventually forming a substantial shade tree rather than a small ornamental. Its heavily textured, velvety white bracts overlap densely for a profuse spring bloom, aging to creamy white as they mature. The hybrid parentage confers strong resistance to dogwood anthracnose and dogwood borer, two problems that have limited straight Cornus florida plantings in much of the eastern United States. Give it room to mature to full size, consistent moisture while establishing, and light shade from the hottest afternoon sun in warmer zones.

common_name: Constellation Dogwood (Rutgers Hybrid Upright Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Constellation's low-branching, upright form works well as a specimen or street tree where a fruitless dogwood is preferred.

directions: Another product of the Rutgers dogwood breeding program that crossed native flowering dogwood with kousa dogwood, Constellation forms a low-branched, upright small tree covered in large, showy white bracts each spring. Unlike many dogwoods it sets little to no fruit, an advantage for plantings near walkways or patios where fallen fruit would be a nuisance. Dark green summer foliage turns purplish red in fall, and the hybrid vigor of this selection brings strong resistance to anthracnose and borer damage compared with straight Cornus florida. Water deeply during the establishment period and site it where its eventual 16- to 22-foot height won't crowd nearby structures.
